metadata.description: The Lab Sampling datasets contain relevant information pertaining to USDA lab sampling projects and tasks. The data include, but are not limited to, identifying establishment information, the sampling project, and results from the samples taken. The sampling results are grouped into seven pathogens: generic E. coli, E. coli O157:H7, Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria, and Enterococcus. Samples can be identified by the unique identifiers known as the form_id and sample_number. Each form_id corresponds to an entire sample, while the sample_number corresponds to various tests that can be performed on the sample.
metadata.lab_sampling_tests_structure: Each form_id can have one or multiple sample_number values. The sampling tests and their sample_numbers are structured in a primary-secondary relationship. In most cases, a 'primary' test will be performed first, and a 'secondary' test will be performed based on the results of the primary test. For example, a primary test would be if a sample is tested for the presence of Salmonella. If the result is Negative, this primary test will not have an associated secondary test. If the result is Positive, however, a secondary test will be performed to determine the serotype of the Salmonella isolate. Finally, a 'tertiary' test can be performed as well. Furthering the previous example, once the Salmonella isolate is determined, the allele code will then be entered for that isolate. In this example, the secondary test is dependent upon the primary test, and the tertiary test is dependent upon the secondary test. This may not always be the case as there do exist 'orphan' secondary/tertiary tests. In most cases, these can be explained by third parties who conduct sampling projects on behalf of the USDA which may not perform the primary tests, or the primary sample data is not received by the USDA.
metadata.disclaimer:
Data postings are part of the Agency's efforts to prevent pathogens from entering the food supply throughout the farm-to-fork continuum. Posting these datasets may help industry identify repetitive subtypes and implement control measures. It may allow researchers to identify trends to address basic research questions or to develop new diagnostics or therapies, such as vaccines. 
 These datasets are posted for informational purposes only and are not sufficient to determine if there is an association between multiple samples. Therefore, this data should not be used to identify foodborne illness outbreaks, associate samples with foodborne illness outbreaks or determine whether two or more samples are causally related. Further epidemiologic information is needed to determine if there is an association among the non-clinical isolates and human illnesses.
metadata.json_file_format: This dataset is available in an open, non-proprietary, publicly accessible JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format consistent with requirements set by the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 (https://www.congress.gov/115/plaws/publ435/PLAW-115publ435.pdf). Additional information can be found on the FSIS Laboratory Sampling Data web page (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/science-data/data-sets-visualizations/laboratory-sampling-data).
metadata.tidy_data_format:
The Lab Sampling datasets will adhere to tidy data principles. Tidy data is a framework for standardizing a dataset which maps its meaning to its structure: each variable forms a column, each observation forms a row, each value forms a cell, and each observational unit forms a dataset. One of the major efforts in tidying the Lab Sampling data included expanding sampling tests into unique columns. Doing so allows the data to adhere to the aforementioned tidy data principles: each row is a unique sample_number, each column is a test that is performed on the sample, and each cell is the result of that test, if performed. More information pertaining to tidy data principles can be found here: https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v059i10. 
 Additionally, to maintain consistency across datasets, FSIS will begin utilizing 'snake_case' for all variable names. This format consists of all lowercase letters, and every space is replaced by an underscore. Some examples include: establishment_id, establishment_name, salmonella_serotype, allele_code, etc. 
 Data will be broken out by fiscal year (FY), starting with data from FY14 (starting on October 1, 2013) through the most recent FY. Files will be updated on a quarterly basis.
metadata.primary_secondary_data_products: In rare cases, a single secondary test can be performed multiple times. This occurs when multiple Salmonella serotypes are identified from a single positive Salmonella sample. If this was placed into a single dataset, this would violate tidy data principles as this would cause two rows to have the same primary sample_number value (the same observation in multiple rows). To fix this, the datasets were split into a primary dataset and a secondary dataset. The primary dataset contains only the primary test information, one per row. The secondary dataset contains all the secondary test information, one per row. The secondary dataset also contains all tertiary test information because in no cases can a single tertiary test be performed multiple times, so the secondary and tertiary information can safely be placed in the same row with no issues.
metadata.joining_primary_secondary_data_products:
In order to properly join the primary and secondary datasets to see all available data, use the column form_id as the primary/foreign key, and utilize a full outer join (sometimes simply called an outer join). A full outer join is needed to ensure all orphan secondary samples are also included in the final result. For example, a simple SQL query would look like this: 
 <  SELECT * FROM pathogen_primary_test ppt FULL JOIN pathogen_secondary_test pct ON pct.form_id = ppt.form_id  > 
 The pathogen_primary_test dataset also includes the Establishment ID from the establishment where the sample was taken. Use this variable (in this dataset named 'establishment_id' with lowercase letters and an underscore) to join the pathogen_primary_test dataset to other FSIS datasets.

data_product_update_information.information: FSIS may modify the structure and information provided within this data asset over time to accurately reflect changes in FSIS policy or sampling methods without seeking public comments. Information that may be updated includes, but is not limited to, project codes, variables, and tolerance levels. Data users may see differences between data during different time periods due to program variations. FSIS will announce and changes in a Constituent Update and will note the update in the data_product_update_information section.

metadata.fsis_number_wgs_information: The FSIS number is a unique identifier for retrieving whole genome sequence data from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) Pathogen Detection Isolates Browser (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/isolates/). The allele codes included in this dataset provide a convenient naming method for reporting Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data. Because allele codes can change over time as more WGS data becomes available, a date stamp allows the data to be used in reports. Due to the increased discriminatory power of WGS, FSIS transitioned away from Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE) to using WGS as the typing tool in 2019 along with CDC and public health partners. The PFGE data is included for transparency purposes and is not intended to be used in any investigative processes through any data releases.
metadata.outbreak_information: FSIS, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and other public health partners monitor WGS information gathered from samples in real time and use sophisticated epidemiological tools to identify whether the cumulative findings might signal a foodborne illness outbreak. Outbreaks identified through this process are announced to the public through CDC's website and FSIS' Outbreak Response Page (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/isolates/). The FSIS investigative process is described in FSIS Directive 8080.3 (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/policy/fsis-directives/8080.3).
metadata.data_product_overview: This dataset contains data from three types of RTE projects. FSIS collects RTE product samples both randomly (RTEPROD_RAND) and using a risk-based algorithm (RTEPROD_RISK). In addition, this dataset includes the results of FSIS' Intensified Verification Testing (IVT) sampling program for ready-to-eat products. The IVT sampling program collects product, food contact, and environmental (non-food contact) samples. This sampling is typically done 'for cause' (e.g., positive sample results). IVTs may also be scheduled due to repetitive occurrences of noncompliance in the establishment's Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) control program, including sanitation issues. IVTs are performed in response to Salmonella positives as well. Finally, the dataset contains sampling results of FSIS' routine risk-based Listeria monocytogenes (RLm) sampling program that was designed to detect Listeria monocytogenes in the environment of a production establishment. The RLm sampling program collects a set of product, food contact, and environmental (non-food contact) samples at an establishment, which is done in conjunction with a risk-based Public Health Risk Evaluation (PHRE) or a routine Food Safety Assessment (FSA). A set of samples collected at an establishment is sent to one of three FSIS laboratories for analysis. See FSIS Directive 10,240.5, Revision 3 (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/policy/fsis-directives/10240.5) for additional details.
metadata.notes_limitations:
Information about FSIS sampling laboratories and procedures can be found on the FSIS website on the Laboratories & Procedures (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/science-data/laboratories-procedures) web page and the Microbiology Laboratory Guidebook (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/news-events/publications/microbiology-laboratory-guidebook) (MLG) web page. 
 NULL values indicate that the specific variable is not available for that record. 
 Samples analyzed for Salmonella and Campylobacter may lack results for one organism. Lack of analysis for one organism is due to either insufficient volume to perform both analyses or not being analyzed due to not meeting all receipt temperature criteria; MLG Chapter 1.01 (https://www.fsis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media_file/2022-03/MLG_1.01.pdf). Delays in sample analysis can occur when a sample is non-viable or when there is a need to repeat the WGS analysis. 
 When a sample screens positive for a pathogen, there normally is only one isolate (e.g., subtype determined using serology [serotype], PFGE, antibiotic resistance, allele code, or whole genome sequence) derived from laboratory confirmation procedures. During such procedures, the enrichment broth is streaked on agar plates, and those plates are subsequently examined for typical pathogen colonies. The laboratory staff ordinarily picks no more than one typical isolated colony from any one plate. On very rare occasions, more than one typical colony may be picked for confirmation. In such circumstances, the multiple isolate data (e.g., Salmonella serotype) are separated by a semicolon. 
 Confirmed positive bacterial isolates can become unsuitable for additional testing during shipping, transfer, or storage. This result is final as further characterization cannot be performed. When this occurs, the isolate characterization result fields (e.g., serotype, antimicrobial resistance, allele code) will be populated with 'Final result - characterization not available' and the FSIS Number will be reported as 'FSISNOTSEQ'. 
 WGS data must be interpreted within the context of how it will be used, e.g., to detect outbreaks or contamination events. Additional corroborating information, including case-patient food exposure and product distribution records, may be necessary to properly interpret the WGS data. 
 The product_name is a free-text entry, and the sample_source_name is selected from a structured list. Due to these differing collection methods, the two fields may not always correspond, and some values may be blank. The product_name field is only applicable to product sampling projects and will remain blank for environmental and other non-product sampling projects. All personally identifiable information (e.g., names, phone numbers, etc.) and any corporate proprietary information have been redacted and replaced with '[REDACTED]'.

The production alternative used by the establishment to produce the product that was sampled. Possible Alternatives: 
 ALT 1 - The establishment uses a post-lethality treatment (PLT) to reduce or eliminate Lm in the product and an antimicrobial agent or process (AMAP) to limit or suppress growth of Lm in the product. 
 ALT 2 PLT (Post-Lethality Treatment) - The establishment uses a PLT to reduce or eliminate Lm in the product. 
 ALT 2 AMAP (Anti-Microbial Agent or Process) - The establishment uses AMAP to limit or suppress growth of Lm in the product. 
 ALT 3 - The establishment relies on sanitation alone to control Lm in the processing environment and on the product.
Indicates if the corresponding sample was unable to be analyzed. A value of '00' indicates the sample was analyzed.
The reason explaining why a sample was not analyzed.
Microbiology Test: The result of the analysis for Salmonella in the sample. Negative indicates Salmonella was not found in the sample. Positive indicates Salmonella was found in the sample.
Indicates if the corresponding test was canceled. The value will be the reason for the cancellation.

Microbiology Test (Unit: per gram) - Result of the analysis to estimate the population density of viable Salmonella. Results are reported as an estimate of the most probable number (MPN/g) of observed positive growth responses in a standard dilution series of sample inoculum. Salmonella MPN was discontinued in March 2020.
Indicates if the corresponding test was canceled. The value will be the reason for the cancellation.

Microbiology Test (5 sets of 3 tubes): Result of the analysis to estimate the population density of viable Salmonella. Results are reported as the number of tubes that were observed to have positive growth responses in a standard dilution series of sample inoculum placed into a set number of culture media tubes. Salmonella most probable number (MPN) was discontinued in March 2020.
Indicates if the corresponding test was canceled. The value will be the reason for the cancellation.

Microbiology Test: Qualitative result of the analysis to estimate the population density of viable Salmonella. Salmonella most probable number (MPN) was discontinued in March 2020. 
 Positive = observed growth responses in at least one culture tube of a standard dilution series of the sample inoculum. 
 Negative = no growth observed.

A combination of the pathogen and the primary sample number. The primary sample number is known as the 'sample_number' in the primary dataset. The pathogen is indicated by a four-letter code:

The FSIS number is a unique identifier for retrieving whole genome sequence data from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) Pathogen Detection Isolates Browser (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/isolates/). NCBI developed the Browser to help users learn about the sequences they contribute. NCBI has provided a video introduction (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T8HluuzOb5c) to this browser, and this document contains a table (ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser_information) outlining information available in NCBI'S Pathogen Detection Isolates Brower for additional reference. 
  
 The allele codes included in this dataset provide a convenient naming method for reporting Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data. Because allele codes can change over time as more WGS data becomes available, a date stamp allows the data to be used in reports. FSIS, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and other public health partners monitor WGS information gathered from samples in real time and use sophisticated epidemiological tools to identify whether the cumulative findings might signal a foodborne illness outbreak. Outbreaks identified through this process are announced to the public through CDC's website and FSIS' Outbreak Response Page. The FSIS investigative process is described in FSIS Directive 8080.3.

The first part of the composite allele code assigned by CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html). The version is comprised of the organism and the naming script used. When PulseNet is unable to assign an allele code, the entry will be: Allele Code Ineligible.

A code assigned by CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html) based on the number of differences in pre-defined genes in the WGS data. When PulseNet is unable to assign an allele code, the entry will be: Allele Code Ineligible.
The date when FSIS retrieved the salmonella_allele_code from CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html).
A unique identifier for retrieving raw sequencing data and alignment information from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) database.
A unique identifier that links to isolate metadata. Data users can use the accession number to search for isolates with the NCBI Isolate Browser from the National Institute of Health (NIH).
A unique identifier for retrieving biological source materials data from the BioProject database from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) database.
Subtyping scheme based on 7 housekeeping genes used to group isolates at a broad level (more discriminatory than species but not necessarily serotype).

Antimicrobial resistance genes identified in the Salmonella isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

Stress resistance genes identified in the Salmonella isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

Virulence resistance genes identified in the Salmonella isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

Follow-up Microbiology Test - Salmonella Serotype. The name of the distinct variation of the tested species of bacteria. A list of the serotypes that are more commonly associated with human illness can be found on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) web site on their National Salmonella Surveillance (https://www.cdc.gov/nationalsurveillance/salmonella-surveillance.html) web page.

The specific primary pattern identified from Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE), which is the laboratory technique used to produce a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) fingerprint for a group of the same type of bacteria. FSIS discontinued PFGE characterization in March 2019 and replaced the technique with the more modern whole genome sequencing (WGS) characterization.

The specific secondary pattern identified from Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE), which is the laboratory technique used to produce a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) fingerprint for a group of the same type of bacteria. FSIS discontinued PFGE characterization in March 2019 and replaced the technique with the more modern whole genome sequencing (WGS) characterization.

Indicates if the actual resistance point of the given pathogen to the given antimicrobial is greater than, less than, or equal to the accompanying Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) value. For example, if the MIC value is 256 and the operator is  >, then the organism was resistant to a concentration of greater than 256 for the given antimicrobial.

The minimum tested concentration (μg/ml) of the antimicrobial drug found to completely inhibit growth of the isolate. If the MIC value recorded is the lowest concentration in the testing range, the MIC value is determined to be equal to or less than the tested concentration. If the MIC value recorded is the highest concentration in the testing range, the MIC value is either equal to or greater than the tested concentration. The concentration ranges for testing each pathogen-antimicrobial combination can be found here Concentration Ranges Used for Susceptibility Testing (https://www.fda.gov/media/108187/download?attachment).

Yes - The salmonella isolate's MIC value for the antimicrobial drug meets the resistant breakpoint criteria and is considered resistant based on AST.  
  No - The salmonella isolate's MIC value for the antimicrobial drug does not meet the resistant breakpoint criteria and is not considered resistant based on AST.  
 The clinical breakpoints can be found in the 2021 NARMS Interpretive Criteria for Susceptibility Testing.

The first part of the composite allele code assigned by CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html). The version is comprised of the organism and the naming script used. When PulseNet is unable to assign an allele code, the entry will be: Allele Code Ineligible.

A code assigned by CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html) based on the number of differences in pre-defined genes in the WGS data. When PulseNet is unable to assign an allele code, the entry will be: Allele Code Ineligible.
The date when FSIS retrieved the listeria_allele_code from CDC-PulseNet (https://www.cdc.gov/pulsenet/index.html).
A unique identifier for retrieving raw sequencing data and alignment information from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) database.
A unique identifier that links to isolate metadata. Data users can use the accession number to search for isolates with the NCBI Isolate Browser from the National Institute of Health (NIH).
A unique identifier for retrieving biological source materials data from the BioProject database from the National Center for Biotechnology and Information (NCBI) database.
Subtyping scheme based on 7 housekeeping genes used to group isolates at a broad level (more discriminatory than species but not necessarily serotype).

Antimicrobial resistance genes identified in the Listeria monocytogenes isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

Stress resistance genes identified in the Listeria monocytogenes isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

Virulence resistance genes identified in the Listeria monocytogenes isolate by NCBI using AMRFinderPlus tool (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/antimicrobial-resistance/AMRFinder/). NCBI's AMRFinderPlus tool relies on NCBI's curated Reference Gene Database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/refgene/#).

The specific primary pattern identified from Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE), which is the laboratory technique used to produce a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) fingerprint for a group of the same type of bacteria. FSIS discontinued PFGE characterization in March 2019 and replaced the technique with the more modern whole genome sequencing (WGS) characterization.

The specific secondary pattern identified from Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE), which is the laboratory technique used to produce a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) fingerprint for a group of the same type of bacteria. FSIS discontinued PFGE characterization in March 2019 and replaced the technique with the more modern whole genome sequencing (WGS) characterization.
The non-Listeria Monocytogenes species result

fda_antimicrobial_classification_definit.fda_class_definition_footnote: FDA Classification is taken from Appendix A of the FDA Guidance for Industry #152 dated October 23, 2003 (https://public4.pagefreezer.com/browse/FDA/30-11-2022T08:34/https:/www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cvm-gfi-152-evaluating-safety-antimicrobial-new-animal-drugs-regard-their-microbiological-effects). The FDA is in the process of updating Guidance for Industry #152, and the new draft guidance is available on their website (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cvm-gfi-152-evaluating-safety-antimicrobial-new-animal-drugs-regard-their-microbiological-effects). FSIS will update the table accordingly once the FDA implements the updated guidance.

fda_class_definition_table.definition: Antimicrobial drugs which meet BOTH criteria 1 and 2 in Appendix A of the FDA Guidance for Industry #152 are considered critically important to human medical therapy.
Antimicrobial drugs which meet EITHER criteria 1 or 2 in Appendix A of the FDA Guidance for Industry #152 are considered highly important to human medical therapy.
Antimicrobial drugs which meet EITHER criterion 3 and/or 4 and/or 5 in Appendix A of the FDA Guidance for Industry #152 are considered important to human medical therapy.
Antimicrobial drugs which are not given a classification in FDA's Guidance for Industry #152 (dated October 23, 2003).

fda_antimicrobial_drug_classification_ta.Notes: FSIS has classified drugs approved for animal use only using the same classification that FDA has designated for drugs in the same antimicrobial class that are approved for human use.
FSIS has classified drugs approved for animal use only using the same classification that FDA has designated for drugs in the same antimicrobial class that are approved for human use.

ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser.Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNP) clu: A SNP cluster is a group of isolates whose genomes are closely related. In the Pathogen Detection Browser this element will contain a link that opens a new page with information about closely related sequences in the database.
ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser.Min-same or Min-diff: Minimum SNP distance from the query isolate to one of the same or a different isolation type. Isolation types are clinical (including human or animal) or environmental (including food).
ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser.BioSample: Further information (metadata) pertaining to the sample from which the sequence was isolated.
ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser.Assembly: Technical information pertaining to the sequence.
ncbi_pathogen_detection_isolates_browser.AMR Genotype: Information pertaining to antimicrobial resistant (AMR) genes found in the isolate sequence. Additional information about each AMR gene in this field is provided by a Reference Gene Catalog (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pathogens/isolates%23/refgene/). Note: Empty cells do not necessarily indicate a lack of AMR genes.
